questions.q: A train fails between stations. What is the universal emergency sequence that should guide every action?
options: Protect, inform, assess, act, evacuate if needed, restore, then report
Inform, evacuate, protect, restore, report, assess
Restore, report, protect, evacuate, inform, assess
Act, evacuate, restore, protect, report, inform
questions.explain: This order protects life first and paperwork last — every emergency answer in operations follows it.

questions.q: In any emergency, what comes first — passengers, property or the timetable?
options: The timetable, then property, then life
Safety of life, then property, then the timetable
Property, then life, then the timetable
All three carry equal priority
questions.explain: Life before property, property before timetable — always. Restoring service never outranks protecting people.

questions.q: A train loses power and stops in a section. The operator's very first actions are to:
options: Open all doors so passengers can leave quickly
Start walking passengers towards the next station
Secure the train with brakes and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) of the exact location, condition and passenger load
Leave the cab to inspect the track ahead
questions.explain: A secured train and an informed Operations Control Centre (OCC) come before everything else — OCC cannot plan a rescue it does not know about.

questions.q: After reporting a failed train, the operator should next:
options: Try any repair he personally thinks may work, without a time limit
Wait silently without trying anything at all
Ask passengers to push the train to the next station
Attempt only the authorised troubleshooting and restart steps, guided by Operations Control Centre (OCC), within the allowed time
questions.explain: Troubleshooting is authorised and time-bound — many failures clear here, but endless trying delays the rescue decision.

questions.q: Who takes the final decision on how a failed train and its passengers will be recovered?
options: The train operator alone
Operations Control Centre (OCC), choosing between self-recovery, rescue by another train, or evacuation
The senior-most passenger on board
The nearest station master alone
questions.explain: The operator reports and secures; Operations Control Centre (OCC) sees the whole network picture and authorises the recovery plan.

questions.q: A rescue train is sent to a failed train mainly to:
options: Carry officials to inspect the failed train
Deliver spare parts to the depot
Run the failed train's remaining timetable trips
Move the failed train, or transfer its passengers under Operations Control Centre (OCC) control
questions.explain: Rescue working is a planned degraded operation — the rescue train pushes/pulls the failed train or takes its passengers.

questions.q: Which is the most preferred way to get passengers off a failed train?
options: Move the train to a station platform and detrain them there
Detrain them onto the track between stations
Detrain them through the tunnel walkway
Ask them to climb down wherever the train stopped
questions.explain: A platform gives light, space, staff and help — so reaching a station is always the first preference.

questions.q: If a failed train cannot reach a station, the next preferred evacuation route is:
options: Directly onto the open track
Through the driver's cab window
Along the walkway or through cross-passages, under Operations Control Centre (OCC) control
Over the roof of the train
questions.explain: Walkways and cross-passages are designed evacuation routes — controlled and protected, unlike the open track.

questions.q: Track-level evacuation of passengers is treated as:
options: The first and fastest option
The normal method in tunnels
Something passengers may start themselves
The last resort, used only when no safer option exists
questions.explain: The track has live rails, other trains and poor footing — it is used only when every safer route is ruled out.

questions.q: Before any track-level evacuation begins, which condition is essential?
options: The next train has passed the section
Passengers have collected all their luggage
Trains are stopped on the affected lines and traction power is confirmed isolated where required
The media has been informed about the incident
questions.explain: Nobody steps onto a track until movements are stopped and the power status is confirmed safe under Operations Control Centre (OCC) authority.

questions.q: During an evacuation, why are staff positioned along the route to the safe place?
options: To check tickets of evacuating passengers
To guide passengers, assist the vulnerable and keep the flow moving in one direction
To photograph the evacuation for records
To count the seats left empty in the train
questions.explain: Positioned staff turn a crowd into an orderly flow — like ushers in a dark cinema hall.

questions.q: Passengers must never be allowed to self-evacuate from a failed train because:
options: Uncontrolled movement on a live railway can kill — evacuation must be authorised and protected
It makes the operator's report longer
It delays the rescue train's paperwork
Self-evacuation is not mentioned in the timetable
questions.explain: People forcing doors onto live tracks have died in real railways — control is what keeps evacuation safe.

questions.q: Why does the crew keep passengers informed with announcements during a long train failure?
options: Announcements repair the train faster
Passengers are legally entitled to a commentary
Information prevents panic, and panic injures more people than most failures do
Silence would damage the train's Public Address (PA) system
questions.explain: An informed passenger stays seated and calm; a silent train fills with rumours and fear.

questions.q: During controlled detrainment, who is assisted first?
options: Children, the elderly, wheelchair users and others who need help
Passengers holding season tickets
Passengers sitting nearest the doors
Staff travelling off duty
questions.explain: Vulnerability decides priority — those who cannot manage ladders and walkways alone are helped first.

questions.q: Passengers are detrained from a failed train through:
options: Any window they can open
The emergency hammer exit in the roof
Doors they force open themselves
The designated door, using the ladder or ramp provided, with staff at the detrainment point
questions.explain: One controlled exit point with staff and equipment is safer than many improvised exits.

questions.q: After all passengers have left a failed train, what must be done before the section can reopen?
options: The train is cleaned for the next service
The train and the route are checked and everyone is counted clear
Tickets of all passengers are collected
A press note about the incident is issued
questions.explain: Count out must equal count in — a section never reopens on assumption.

questions.q: Once evacuation is complete, the failed train is:
options: Moved to the depot when it is safe to do so
Left in the section permanently
Pushed into the nearest tunnel cross-passage
Opened for passengers to collect luggage at leisure
questions.explain: Clearing the failed train from the running line, when safe, is part of completing the recovery.

questions.q: A passenger tries to force open a door of a failed train in a tunnel. The crew should:
options: Help him open it to keep him calm
Ignore it as a minor matter
Stop him, reassure passengers and repeat clear announcements on what is happening and what to do
Unlock all doors to release the pressure
questions.explain: Forced doors lead to the track danger — calm, clear information is the tool that stops it.

questions.q: Which information does Operations Control Centre (OCC) most need in the operator's first report of a train failure?
options: The operator's duty roster for the week
Exact location, train condition and passenger load
The names of all passengers on board
The weather at the depot that morning
questions.explain: Location, condition and load decide the rescue plan — Operations Control Centre (OCC) plans from these three facts.

questions.q: Why is a fixed time limit set for troubleshooting a failed train?
options: Because spare parts expire after that time
To give the rescue train time to be cleaned
Because passengers stop listening after that time
So that rescue or evacuation is not delayed while attempts continue endlessly
questions.explain: Batteries, patience and conditions all run down — a time limit forces a timely decision.

questions.q: Two trains are involved: one failed, one sent to assist. Their coupling and movement must be:
options: Decided between the two operators by phone
Done at full line speed to save time
Carried out only under Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorisation and the prescribed rescue procedure
Left to the senior operator's judgement alone
questions.explain: Rescue movements are degraded operations with their own rules — unauthorised coupling can create a second incident.

questions.q: In a tunnel, why is detraining passengers at a station better than along the tunnel walkway?
options: The walkway is reserved for staff only
The station offers staff, light, medical help and safe exits all in one place
Stations are closer to the depot
Passengers prefer stations for shopping
questions.explain: Every facility a passenger may need exists at a station and almost none exist in a tunnel.

questions.q: A failed train can move slowly on its own power. Operations Control Centre (OCC) will most likely direct it to:
options: The nearest station, to detrain passengers safely at the platform
The middle of the next tunnel
Continue its full journey regardless
The depot with passengers still on board
questions.explain: If it can crawl, it crawls to a platform — detrainment there is the safest ending.

questions.q: What should passengers be clearly told NOT to do during a train evacuation?
options: Remain seated until instructed
Listen to crew announcements
Help children and elderly passengers
Force doors, enter the track on their own, or go back for luggage
questions.explain: The NOT list prevents the three classic killers: forced doors, lone track entry and luggage delays.

questions.q: Why is the passenger count maintained during and after an evacuation?
options: For ticket refund calculations
To prove nobody is left behind in the train or along the route
For the catering contractor's records
To update the passenger information display
questions.explain: Counting is the safety net — an uncounted evacuation can leave a person behind in a tunnel.

questions.q: A train fails on a viaduct (elevated section). The evacuation principles differ from a tunnel mainly in that:
options: Passengers may jump down as the height is small
No Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorisation is needed on a viaduct
The same controlled method applies — walkway under Operations Control Centre (OCC) control, track level only as a last resort
Evacuation is never permitted on a viaduct
questions.explain: Height changes the route furniture, not the principles: controlled, authorised, protected.

questions.q: During evacuation planning, Operations Control Centre (OCC) briefs the receiving station mainly so that:
options: The station can close its booking office
The station can announce commercial offers
The station master can inform the press first
Staff, first aid and onward arrangements are ready when passengers arrive
questions.explain: A prepared receiving station turns an arrival of hundreds into an orderly handover.

questions.q: The operator of a failed train notices smoke smell while troubleshooting. His priority now:
options: Stop troubleshooting, protect passengers, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately — the incident has changed class
Finish the restart attempt first
Open windows and continue the journey
Ask passengers if they also smell it
questions.explain: A possible fire outranks a failure — the emergency sequence restarts at 'protect and inform'.

questions.q: Why must movements on the adjacent line also be stopped or cautioned during a track evacuation?
options: To give the rescue train a parking place
Passengers near the track could be struck by a train on the neighbouring line
So that the adjacent train's passengers can watch
Because both lines share one driver
questions.explain: Evacuating people stand close to the other line — its trains are a direct danger to them.

questions.q: A controlled evacuation is ordered. Who gives the final 'go' for passengers to start leaving the train?
options: The first passenger who reaches the door
The operator acting entirely on his own
Operations Control Centre (OCC), after the area has been made safe and staff are positioned
The station master of the nearest station by phone to passengers
questions.explain: The go-ahead follows safety confirmation — movements stopped, power dealt with, staff in place.

questions.q: After an evacuation, a passenger reports chest pain at the station. The correct action is:
options: Give first aid, inform Operations Control Centre (OCC)/station control and arrange ambulance/medical handover
Ask him to rest and continue his journey later
Send him back to the train to sit down
Wait for the next scheduled ambulance round
questions.explain: Medical needs found during evacuation are handled as a medical emergency in parallel.

questions.q: Which quality of an evacuation matters most in judging whether it was done well?
options: It finished in the shortest possible time
No train was delayed by it
It required the fewest staff
Everyone reached a safe place, accounted for, without injury — not how fast it was
questions.explain: Order, not speed, is the standard — a fast, chaotic evacuation is a failed one.

questions.q: A train fails just short of a station platform, doors not aligned with the platform. The best course is:
options: Open whichever doors hang over the platform edge
Let agile passengers jump the gap
Follow Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s instruction — move to align if possible, else controlled detrainment by the prescribed method
Ask passengers to pull the train forward
questions.explain: Partial alignment is a trap — improvised jumping causes falls; the prescribed method controls it.

questions.q: During a long failure, the train's batteries mainly serve to:
options: Restart the traction motors repeatedly
Keep lights and ventilation running for a limited period while decisions are taken
Power the train to the next station
Charge passengers' mobile phones
questions.explain: Batteries buy time, not movement — decisions must be completed inside that time.

questions.q: Why does Operations Control Centre (OCC) sometimes choose passenger transfer to a rescue train instead of towing the failed train first?
options: Towing is never permitted in Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS)
The rescue train needs passenger load for balance
Passengers enjoy changing trains
Transfer can clear passengers faster and more safely than a slow tow in some situations
questions.explain: The aim is people to safety first; the failed train can be recovered afterwards.

questions.q: The receiving end of an evacuation route must be a 'safe place'. This means:
options: A place clear of trains, live equipment and the incident itself, where passengers can assemble
Any place outside the train
The nearest road, whatever its traffic
Inside the next train standing in the section
questions.explain: A safe place is defined by what it is clear of — danger must not follow the passengers.

questions.q: An operator secures a failed train. 'Secure' here means:
options: All doors locked with passengers inside permanently
The train's valuables locked in the cab
Brakes applied and the train protected so it cannot move unexpectedly
A security guard posted at each door
questions.explain: A secured train stays where it stopped — no roll-away risk while people move around it.

questions.q: If evacuation is ordered but a few passengers refuse to leave the train, staff should:
options: Leave them and close the evacuation
Persuade calmly, explain the reason, assist them — and report the situation to Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Physically drag them out immediately
Cancel the evacuation for everyone
questions.explain: Refusal is handled by communication and escalation, never by abandonment or force as a first step.

questions.q: The incident log for a train evacuation must finally show:
options: That evacuation is complete, all persons are accounted for and Operations Control Centre (OCC) has logged completion
Only the time the train failed
The list of delayed trains
The names of staff on leave
questions.explain: The log closes the safety loop — completion and accounting are formally recorded.

questions.q: After passengers are evacuated and the line is clear, service recovery begins with:
options: Running extra trains at double speed to catch up
Cancelling the rest of the day's service
Refunding all tickets first
Moving the failed train clear when safe and restoring the section under Operations Control Centre (OCC) direction
questions.explain: Recovery follows the same control: the failed train is cleared, then the timetable is rebuilt.

questions.q: A rescue train has coupled to a failed train and will propel it to the next station. Before the combined unit moves, the crews must complete:
options: A fresh ticket check of all passengers
A brake continuity test — proving the brakes apply and release through the whole combined train from the driving cab in use
A full timetable revision
Repainting of the train number boards
questions.explain: Coupling joins two trains into one machine. A brake continuity test proves the driver of the combined unit can actually brake the whole consist before it moves with or near passengers.

questions.q: In a twin-bore tunnel, cross passages connect the two bores at intervals. During an evacuation from a failed train, their role is to:
options: Store maintenance tools
Let passengers walk from the incident bore into the non-incident bore, which acts as a safe route away from the train
Allow trains to change tunnels
House the signalling equipment
questions.explain: The other bore is the tunnel's built-in escape route. Cross passages turn it into a safe place reachable on foot, under Operations Control Centre (OCC) control and with movements in that bore stopped or controlled.

questions.q: A passenger in a failed train presses the emergency intercom/alarm. The correct handling is:
options: Ignore it — passengers always panic
The operator answers, learns the problem, informs the Operations Control Centre (OCC) and announcements are made; the alarm is never treated as a joke until checked
The train doors open automatically at once
The passenger is fined before anyone listens
questions.explain: The emergency intercom is the passengers' interface with the crew. Every activation is answered and reported to the Operations Control Centre (OCC) — it may be the first warning of a medical case or smoke.

questions.q: A train fails on a steep gradient (slope). The extra danger the operator must guard against while securing the train is:
options: Passengers getting bored
The train rolling back or running away down the gradient if brakes are not fully applied and the train properly secured
Loss of mobile phone signal
The air-conditioning stopping
questions.explain: On a gradient, gravity is a standing threat. Full brake application and proper securing come before troubleshooting — a rolling train turns a failure into a collision.

questions.q: When passengers are detrained onto a trackside walkway, doors are enabled only on the walkway side of the train. This 'side selection' matters because:
options: It saves battery power
Opening doors on the wrong side would put passengers onto the adjacent track or into a drop, instead of onto the safe walkway
Passengers prefer one side of the train
It makes counting passengers faster
questions.explain: Only the safe side is ever opened. Side selection by the operator, confirmed with the Operations Control Centre (OCC), is what keeps an evacuation route safe instead of creating a second accident.
